demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: The rain falls steadily the afternoon the tempered glass partition gives way. Arin is twenty-three, and she traces the fracture line in her mind with her thumb when she thinks no one is watching. She routes display cables behind the modular test wall in the co-working studio where she maps interface prototypes. A loose support bracket, missed during her morning inspection, shifts under her weight. The glass shatters forward. Her colleague, David, does not hear the snap over the studio's ambient audio. By the time he cries out, the lower pane pins his right shin. The ambulance sirens wake her at 3:14 a.m., exactly as they did that afternoon, her body already taut before her eyes open. She tells me about the waiting room first, then the sterile hospital corridor, then the quiet apartment she and her husband, Sameer, move into six months ago. Now, the past bleeds into the present through what she refuses to name. She jumps when her coffee maker clicks. She has stopped taking the subway, preferring the long walk across town, because the sudden braking of the train mimics the impact sound. At night, the ceiling fan's oscillation becomes a slow-motion replay of the glass tipping. She sleeps on the floor near the bedroom door, Sameer's breathing steady beside her, while she counts the seconds between heartbeats until the adrenaline fades. Her work as a UX designer has turned into a daily negotiation with guilt. She sits across from her client's prototype screens, mapping user flows, but every "error state" prompt feels like an indictment. She overchecks her own code, re-routes pathways three times, and leaves the office only after her teammates have gone home. The studio manager stops asking her to lead client demos. She does not blame him. When she walks past reflective surfaces, she does not see her own face; she sees David's expression in the first second after the glass breaks. She drafts apology letters she will never send, deleting them the moment her fingers hover over the "send" key. Her mother calls twice a week, leaving voice messages in Urdu about patience and divine timing. Arin saves them in a folder she does not open. She loves Sameer, and he has been steadfast, but his quiet reassurances sometimes tighten her chest. At twenty-three, she expects marriage to be a foundation, not another weight to carry. When he tries to hold her during a panic spike, she goes rigid, convinced her breath will stop or her thoughts will spill out and contaminate him. She eats mostly plain rice and lentils, the way her grandmother taught her to ground herself, but the taste sits heavy in her stomach. In our third session, she describes a design sprint where a colleague jokes about a "system crash." Arin's pen snaps. She apologizes to the pen, then to the room, then to the empty corner where she imagines the glass might still be waiting to fall. Her shoulders remain hunched, even in the quiet of my office. She maps interfaces for a living, optimizing navigation, reducing friction, anticipating where users will stumble. Yet she cannot design a path through her own mind. When I ask what she wants to change first, she looks at her hands, turning them over as if examining old glass shards, and says she just wants to stop bracing for the next break.
